item.title: The Oxbow
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: Full title: View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm. Cole, the English-born founder of the Hudson River School — America's first homegrown art movement — split this canvas diagonally into a national question. On the left: wilderness, storm-blasted trees, dark weather, the sublime American wild. On the right: sunlit, cultivated river valley, farms and smoke plumes, the pastoral future. The retreating thunderstorm draws the border between them. Painted while Cole was working on his moralizing cycle The Course of Empire, it asks the same question in a single view: is civilization's advance a blessing, and what is lost as the axe moves west? Cole's ambivalence was genuine — he loved the settled valley and mourned the forest. American landscape painting, and in some real sense American environmental thought, begins with this hinge of a picture.
item.lookFor: On the hillside across the river, the cleared patches of forest have long been said to spell crude Hebrew letters reading 'Noah' — upside down, 'Shaddai,' the Almighty. Whether Cole meant it remains one of American art's best arguments.
